In Sheikha's house there was a big copper pot that her mother had inherited from her grandmother, and there was no other pot like it in the whole neighbourhood.

Whenever someone had a wedding, or guests, or Eid, they would knock on the door and say, "Lend us the big pot."

Sheikha was the one who carried it to whoever asked for it. Then she would bring it back black from the fire, and sit with her mother scrubbing it with sand until it shone.

One day, as she scrubbed, she said, "Our pot is in every house except ours!"

One day at noon, the pearl-diving ships came back to the shore. Ghanem, the neighbours' boy, ran to Sheikha's house and said, "My father is back, and the men from the ship are with him. My mother says: lend us the big pot."

Sheikha looked at the pot shining in the corner of the house. She had worked so hard scrubbing it the day before.

She said, "My mother is asleep, and I won't give it without her permission." But she knew her mother had never once turned anyone away.

Then she shut the door, went back to the pot, and sat down beside it.

A little later, Sheikha went up to the roof. In the neighbours' house she saw Umm Ghanem cooking rice in three small pots, putting them on the fire one after another, while the men waited in the sitting room.

The rice burned in one of them. Sheikha came down from the roof, and she did not look at the big pot.

When the sun began to go down, her mother woke up and found that the fire in the stove had gone out. She said, "Sheikha, take the little clay fire-pan and bring an ember from Umm Ghanem's house."

Sheikha stood at the door, then walked slowly to the neighbours' house, as if her feet did not want to walk.

Ghanem opened the door. When he saw the fire-pan in her hand, he took it and went inside. Then he came back with red embers in it, and with a plate of rice and fish too.

He said, "This is from the guests' lunch. My mother sent it for your mother."

Sheikha did not take the plate. She said in a quiet voice, "I'm the one who kept the pot from you, Ghanem."

Ghanem said, "I know. But an ember doesn't make our fire any smaller." Then he laughed and said, "And the pot wouldn't have got any smaller if it had cooked at our house for one day."

Sheikha took the fire-pan and the plate, went home and lit the fire, and told her mother everything.

Then she got up, carried the big pot to Umm Ghanem's house, and said, "Keep it as long as your guests are with you. When they leave, I'll come and carry it back."

Then Eid came, and the big pot went round every house in the neighbourhood, and each time Sheikha carried it without complaining.

﴿فَوَيْلٌ لِّلْمُصَلِّينَ ۝ الَّذِينَ هُمْ عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ سَاهُونَ ۝ الَّذِينَ هُمْ يُرَاءُونَ ۝ وَيَمْنَعُونَ الْمَاعُونَ﴾

📖 Al-Ma'un 4–7. The commentators mention that al-ma'un is what people lend one another, such as the pot, the bucket and the axe. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.
